items.summary: A charcoal cutaway barn: a turkey professor points at a chart of sunrise feeding times while, inside, a farmer sharpens an axe beside roasting pans./images/team-explanation.webp/images/team-explanation.webp There are two major ways of assessing the quality of our understanding of a phenomenon: Pre...
items.full_text:
There are two major ways of assessing the quality of our understanding of a phenomenon: Prediction, and Explanation.
Prediction feels extremely powerful because it seems to be proving its deep understanding by having reality speak on its behalf. You want proof that I understand how the planets move? Well let me tell you exactly where Jupiter will be in the sky on an arbitrary day.
That's powerful indeed.
But David Deutsch has an idea that I think is even more powerful, which is Explanation. And he uses a brilliant example to demonstrate why it's superior to Prediction, though the example itself comes from Bertrand Russell.
He asks us to imagine a turkey on a turkey farm in the United States who holds a scientific lecture for a number of his fellow turkeys on the farm.
To prove he understands the farm, where they've all been for the last 9 months and it's currently early November, he is asked to predict the feeding time on November 25th of this year. And then December 12th.
The turkey professor pulls out a whiteboard and proceeds to map out all the data he has on feeding times, and says confidently that on November 25th, they'll be fed right after sunrise. And he says he knows this is true because he has clear data that nobody can refute.
Day after day he is proven right, and he ultimately convinces everyone he's correct.
But despite all this data, and accuracy, and precision that he's provided, this understanding lacks a critical component. He doesn't have an explanation for "why" they are fed every day after sunrise.
Turns out this is critical information that will drastically affect the accuracy of his predictions.
On November 25th, it turns out, they are not in fact fed after sunrise. Because all those turkeys are dead: killed the day before for Thanksgiving.
He had great data about sunrises and feeding times, but he didn't have the crucial fact that they were turkeys on a turkey farm.
In other words, he could predict parts of the system, but he couldn't explain why it worked the way it did. And in this way, according to David Deutsch, Prediction is subordinate and inferior to Explanation as a way of understanding the world.
The system is not bidirectional, and this one-way function further illustrates why one is better than the other. With Explanation you can usually make predictions, but with predictions alone you often lack an explanation for why they're accurate.
This is why I prioritize high-quality explanations of things. And it's why I so highly value the intelligence of frontier AI. When a modern AI is used properly, it's able to produce extraordinary explanations of nearly anything. And at any level of abstraction, from mathematics and bits and bytes, to extremely concise prose.
One of my favorite AI skills I've ever made (in 2024 via Fabric) is called 5 Levels, which in LifeOS you hit via the /ws shortcut (for /WordSummary).
It takes any idea and explains it to you at n levels of concision.

I’ve been having an almost-debate with Matt Pocock for a while about the best way to do spec driven development.
Matt is a brilliant old-school developer: a true software engineer. And he’s been using AI to enhance his capabilities to an extraordinary degree. His development skills are spectacular, and have been starred more than almost any other skills repo on GitHub.2
So what’s my disagreement?
Basically I think he is at the top of the mountain for the old way of doing things. He’s got tons of skills and tons of commands that he encourages people to run manually. Having a human in the loop is a major theme for him, which I think is now an anti-pattern.
But his central idea lately has been that the most important thing in a development project is the code itself. That specs are useful and everything, but the code itself is the main artifact. The source of truth for everything.1
I disagree strongly. I think the articulation of what you’re building, and why, is far more important. Basically, the idea. Your intent.
I think the most important thing in any project you’re building with AI (and even without it), from building a web app, to starting a business, to managing a federation of planets, is how completely and accurately you articulate exactly what you want.
To be clear, I’m not saying you need a perfect, crystallized articulation before you start. Nobody has that. We’re human, and what we want gets clearer as we build. My argument is about where that iteration happens: inside the articulation of the ideal state, not in circles around the code. And there are two loops, not one. Your intent and the writing go back and forth as you figure out what you actually want, and the writing and the implementation go back and forth as you build.
I think most of the problems we see with AI in 2026 are misattributed. AI is extraordinary at execution. It’s getting unbelievably great at doing what we ask it to do. More and more of the problems at this point are it executing the job perfectly, and having the result be different than what was in our mind.
But this is a communication problem. It’s an articulation problem.
Authors have this same problem. It’s commonly called Writer’s Blindness. It’s where you think you’re perfectly capturing what’s in your brain, but you’re not. And so the receiver, or the reader, ends up missing information or getting a completely different review than the author intended.
The problem with Matt’s position is that he thinks code is authoritative. It’s actually an abstraction, the same way a painting is an abstraction of what the painter was wanting to convey. It’s an execution. A facsimile. A representation.
But there’s a higher form of this, and that’s writing. And images.
Writing is the closest thing we have to human thought. As I like to tell people all the time, for me writing IS thinking. It’s the closest thing we have, by a wide margin.

On October 27, Salesforce released software that lets it send work to agents built with Microsoft Copilot Studio. That same day, Oracle announced that it was developing a workspace to bring its business applications into ChatGPT. The following day, ServiceNow announced a Control Tower Alliance whose founding members include OpenAI, Anthropic, Amazon Web Services, and NVIDIA.
These companies are helping one another reach their customers while competing to become the supplier those customers depend on to get work done across everything else they own. The partnerships are one of the ways they compete for that role.
For years, a business could buy Microsoft for employees’ everyday work, Salesforce for customer relationships, and Oracle for finance. Those companies already competed in places, but they could also maintain substantial relationships with the same customer by serving different parts of the business.
Agents give them a reason to pursue more of the work between their applications.
In my video on the trillion-dollar fight to run your business, I focused on why Salesforce and Microsoft are suddenly competing over responsibilities that used to be more separate. Here I want to widen the view. Google, Amazon, the AI labs, ServiceNow, the business application companies, and the data platforms all have credible reasons to participate. They bring different advantages, and their partnerships tell us a great deal about what each still needs.
If you buy software, this will help you evaluate what you’re being offered. If you’re the person trying to get work done with it, it will help you explain what your company needs to ask for. The decisions being made under the heading of an “AI control plane” will determine a lot about how useful your agents are allowed to become.
This briefing covers:
- What a control plane actually controls. Six responsibilities to separate, from receiving the request to reviewing performance, so you can see which decisions a product can make about the other products.
- Where each vendor starts. What Microsoft, Salesforce, Google, Amazon, OpenAI, Anthropic, ServiceNow, and the business application companies bring, and what their partnerships say each still needs.
- How to read a partnership announcement. Identify what passes between the companies and which direction the connection runs.
- Eight questions for a vendor meeting. Tests for authority, handoffs, mid-job failure, portability, cost, and availability, run against one real task.
- A brief to send every vendor. One task description that makes every demonstration answer the same questions.
Here’s how the competition breaks down, and how to test any proposal you’re handed.

Black October showed how AI is making it easier to break into websites. At the same time, I want AI to use websites for me—to book flights, buy things, and manage my accounts. Businesses need a way to let my agent do that without giving an attacker the same access.
I expect the internet to become more uneven for agents through 2027. Some businesses will build dependable ways to accept them. Others will let them work through the existing website. Some will refuse them. The companies that make legitimate agent activity easier to recognize and accept will gain power because consumers and businesses both need their help.
I’m bullish on that work. We need it. I also want those connections to be open enough that choosing a different assistant doesn’t mean losing access to the places where we live and work online.
I’ve already run into the practical consequence. An agent can put together a trip and then freeze at the hotel’s booking page. The planning was perfect. The hotel still wouldn’t let the agent finish. Now I have to decide whether to complete the booking myself or choose somewhere my agent can book.
That changes which businesses get my money, because I have to figure out how to shop with my agent. A smarter model isn’t going to unlock a door a business has decided to close.

- What each trust system does. Cloudflare’s signed agents, Google’s AP2, Stripe’s payment tokens, the Visa pilot, and Meta’s Sentinel each answer a different question, and one table shows which.
- Why your agent stopped. The three zones tell you whether to correct the agent, give it better information, approve something, or find another route.

items.full_text:
Procurement teams are trying to fit AI into familiar product and service contracts. Finance needs to establish a return on something whose useful applications are still being discovered. Individuals are looking at what the tools can do and wondering where they fit in a company that hasn’t quite figured this out either.
These problems are connected. We can now buy intelligence and decide where to put it to work. We have acquired an economic input that we don’t yet know how to allocate well.
Imagine approving a company-wide AI subscription. You’ve purchased access to intelligence. That access comes without the knowledge of which customer problem to solve, how to connect the relevant systems, or how to make the resulting service useful enough that customers actually use it. Someone still has to supply all of it.
That deserves the CFO’s attention. It can justify buying more than access to a model, including a deeper partnership with someone who knows how to make the intelligence productive. It also deserves your attention as an individual, because the person who supplies that missing judgment can become responsible for work far beyond what they could personally execute.
We’re becoming managers of intelligence before anyone gives us a management title.
This briefing covers:
- Separate what you’re actually buying. How to pull apart what gets billed, who does the work, and who owns the upside, and when outcome pricing or forward-deployed engineers fit.
- Read the return before the invoice fools you. Why the price shows up before the value does, and how to tell the value your company creates from the value it keeps.
- Make a partner earn its share. The questions to settle before a supplier gets equity or a revenue share, and how to value what your own company brings.
- Become the person who allocates the intelligence. How to direct AI toward problems your company has deferred, and how to make that judgment visible.
- Fund something you couldn’t before. A concrete way for a CEO or CFO to commit people and money to a new revenue opportunity, with clear signals for when to expand or stop.
Now that intelligence is a new economic input, here’s what that means for the contract, the return, the partnership, and your own role.

This has been one of the wildest weeks for internet security I can remember. Emergency PHP fixes affect software beneath millions of websites. A certificate authority’s private keys included the number 4. Microsoft has documented AI-assisted attacks targeting hundreds of organizations.
My read on this moment is simple: agents are becoming a central part of both cyber offense and cyber defense because they’re native to computers. They can read unfamiliar software, form an explanation, test it, discover they’re wrong, and keep going. We have accumulated decades of weaknesses in systems people depend on. We now have machines that can investigate those systems with a persistence and scale that human teams have struggled to afford.
We need the best of that intelligence working for us.
There’s a financial reason to take this seriously, too. An AI service key can give whoever holds it the ability to purchase machine work on your bill. That makes access to your AI account valuable even when the attacker has no interest in your conversations. Your computer, your company’s cloud account, or an old application connection may contain the means to keep somebody else’s operation running.
I expect a rough transition. I also think this can lead to a much more secure internet, because the same persistent investigation can help us find, repair, and remove weaknesses that have survived for years. Getting there requires us to put the tools to work and finish the repairs they uncover.

items.title: What if the inside of an AI turns out to be readable after all? New research suggests it might be, and that could make AI mistakes easier to catch.

items.full_text:
Every time you ask an AI a question, your words set off a new pattern of activity inside a model. The numbers learned during training help determine how that activity moves through the network and which answer comes out.
Researchers can record those calculations. What takes more work is explaining what they mean: which patterns the model recognized, how those patterns affected one another, and which ones actually influenced the answer.
Goodfire’s research is so encouraging because it suggests that many of the components doing this work may be more understandable than we’ve assumed.
That could improve our ability to catch and correct AI failures. But I also want to give you enough of a picture of the machinery to understand the research itself.
Here’s what’s inside:

items.summary: How to find what your agents are consuming, get more work from the machine you own, and choose the right Mac, NVIDIA system, or spare computer when you need more room.
items.full_text:
You’re not the only user of your computer anymore.
If you run agents throughout the day, they may open more browsers, start more processes, and write more files than you do. Then you sit down to do something ordinary, open one more application, and the machine asks you to close something. I’ve had that happen repeatedly. I had a memory crash while working toward a deadline after opening one more program as a human. Everything seemed fine until it wasn’t.
You still own the computer and decide what matters, but you now share its resources with software that does much more than answer questions in a chat window. Your agents have become roommates, and most of us never worked out the house rules.
That explains part of the appeal of buying a bigger machine. A Mac mini, a Studio, an NVIDIA box: more room sounds wonderful when the current arrangement is painful. And sometimes more room is exactly what the work needs. But a faster chip won’t stop a development server from remaining open after a project ends. More memory won’t establish which of twelve document-processing jobs should run first. A larger drive will eventually fill if every experiment keeps its own environment forever.
Before spending money, work out what your agents leave running, what they leave behind, and how much of that activity contributes to work you still want done. Then buy for the demand that remains.
Here’s what’s inside:
- A checkup you can run today. A read-only prompt finds what your agents leave running and what they leave behind, and it reports without changing anything.
- A stop sign for every agent. Each job ends with the result saved somewhere you can find and its leftover servers closed.
- A schedule for the heavy work. Start with one heavy job, then try two, and keep whichever finishes sooner without making the computer miserable to use.
- A second job for your old computer. A spare machine can run the background queue so the new one stays usable, and Tailscale lets you reach it while you’re away.
- The companion guide. The three complete prompts, detailed hygiene instructions, and setup walkthroughs for Ollama, LM Studio, Docker Desktop, and Tailscale.
I’ll show you three worked decisions about keeping, reconfiguring, moving, or replacing a machine, then a way to compare the first-year cost of those choices.

Two months ago, I wrote a blog post about the upcoming changes to Meta ads placement controls. At the time, Meta hadn’t made an official announcement, so my reporting was based on what was publicly available, what Meta said privately, and what I could assume based on what was known.
Two months later, Meta made a public announcement about these changes. Based on this new information, I need to update and correct what was previously known or assumed.
The biggest changes are around two things:
- Impacted campaign objectives
- An update to account-level placement controls
In this post, we’ll discuss the following:
- How ad placement control is changing
- Meta’s recommended alternatives
- How I recommend you approach placement control
Let’s get to it…
1. How Ad Placement Control is Changing
You may have seen this message in the Placements section of the ad set…
Meta is eliminating placement control at the ad set level. That means that you won’t be able to remove individual placements, platforms, or isolate mobile and desktop devices.
The question at the time, though, was about when placement control would be eliminated. I had an internal Meta contact who clarified that this would apply to bottom of funnel campaign objectives only. I took that to mean Sales and Leads.
Now that we have Meta’s official documentation, I need to make a correction. This change applies to the following campaign objectives:
- Sales
- Leads
- App Promotion
- Engagement
I assumed it would apply to Sales and Leads, and I probably should have considered App Promotion as well. But the Engagement objective is what’s most surprising. I’d certainly not call that bottom-of-the-funnel, and it’s an objective where you’d normally want to retain placement control.
So, whether I received bad information, I misinterpreted it, or Meta changed the roadmap, placement control is going away at the ad set level for all but two campaign objectives (Awareness and Traffic).
Note that the performance goal doesn’t matter, according to this official information. You could technically maximize the number of link clicks or landing page views using the Sales objective, and you won’t have the ability to remove placements in the ad set. But if you use these same performance goals with a Traffic campaign, you can.
2. Meta’s Recommended Alternatives
Instead of removing placements in the ad set for these four campaign objectives, Meta recommends you do the following:
Customize media for each placement in Ad creative.
Meta says that you should provide different aspect ratios and tailor your creative to each placement.
Honestly, this is a silly recommendation as an alternative. Yes, you should make sure your creative looks optimal in every placement you’re using. But it hardly solves the problem of not being able to remove placements, if that’s something you’d normally do.
Increase or decrease bids using Placement value rules.

items.title: Choose an Audience for Each Ad Creative
items.summary: Meta is rolling out a feature that lets you choose an audience for each ad creative based on age and gender. Here's how it works... The post Choose an Audience for Each Ad Creative appeared first on Jon Loomer Digital .
items.full_text:
Meta is rolling out a feature that allows advertisers to choose an audience for each ad creative. Since there is documentation, I assume it’s an official feature that’s currently rolling out rather than a test.
It’s honestly a surprising new option, given that Meta keeps taking away control. But at the same time, it could be a good alternative to creating separate ad sets for different age groups, assuming that’s what you’re doing now.
Let’s take a closer look…
Requirements
As far as I can tell, there are no requirements by campaign objective. And every performance goal I tried offered this option as well. There was one minor variation for Sales campaigns, where it’s on by default when you’ve chosen to further limit the reach of your ads (it’s otherwise off by default for other objectives).
It’s also available whether you’re using the new creative workflow (also known as multimedia experience) or the original single media experience. It’s a bit different depending on your setup, so I’ll show examples in this post.
If you follow my instructions and still don’t see it, you just don’t have it yet. Sorry.
Toggle It On
Within the ad set, scroll down to the Audiences section. Click to “further limit the reach of your ads.”
Know that I wouldn’t normally recommend you click this button, especially when running Sales campaigns. And I’m honestly not sure why it’s not just an option by default anyway.
If you’re within a Sales campaign, “Choose an audience for each ad creative” should be toggled on by default at this point.
When using any other campaign objective, it will be off by default and will need to be toggled on.
Hover over the tooltip, and you’ll get additional details…
Here’s what it says:
Set an age and gender for each ad creative to indicate who it’s best suited for. Your ad will be directed towards your selected audience, but may also reach others who are likely to respond.
Something you may have noticed in my screenshots is that age range (only minimum age) and gender are not options for restricting your audience while this feature is toggled on.
Customize With Multimedia Experience
If you have the multimedia experience for ad creation, upload at least one image or video. You should then see this option to “choose an audience for each media.”
You can either click the Edit button there or “customize media” under the Media section.
You’ll see a new category: “Audience for This Media.”
You can then define your audience by age and gender for the specific media you’ve selected. Here’s what Meta says:
This media will be directed towards your selected audience, but may also reach others who are likely to respond.
So note that this isn’t a tight restriction. It kind of sounds like you’re making an audience suggestion for that ad creative.
Because you can upload multiple images and videos for a single ad with the multimedia experience, you can customize the audience for each image or video by age and gender.

items.title: How To Use Decision Models for Evals
items.summary: Decision models have exploded onto the scene recently, starting with TypeSafe’s Jev, followed by Perplexity’s Decider, Liquid’s d1, Cloudflare’s Clef, and OpenAI’s Decisions API 1 . These models promise fast, inexpensive classification. Decision models are an appealing low-cost alternative to LLM judges 2 for automated evals. But whether they’re the right choice depends on the cost, performance, and latency requirements of your use case. We’ve also noticed people using the default decision threshold of 0.50 without checking whether it works well for their task. This can leave a lot of performance on the table. In this post, we’ll start by showing how to tune thresholds to get the best results from decision models. With those thresholds tuned, we’ll compare cost and performance to help you assess which model fits your use case. Finally, we’ll explore how to interpret model scores when deciding whether to act, and how calibration can make them more useful as confidence estimates. What we tested We used 100 traces, or logs of conversations and actions, from an apartment leasing agent. The task is to identify traces containing an error, such as a failed booking or a missed handoff to a human. 3 We used the same dataset and broad failure-finding task in our prior post on automated evals . Here, each decision model returns a failure probability for each trace. We tested Jev 1.13, Perplexity Decider 1.1 27B, Liquid d1 and d1-ultra, Cloudflare Clef Flash, and OpenAI Decisions (GPT-6 Luna) 1 . Each model received the same evaluation criteria. The appendix shows the prompt and the structured version used for Jev. We compare models on two dimensions: Performance: We compare each model’s predictions with traces that people have reviewed and labeled as passing or failing. This measures how well the model catches failures while avoiding false alarms. Cost: We calculate API cost from token usage and the provider’s prices. 4 For brevity, we leave latency aside because it depends on factors outside this experiment’s control. 5 Understanding decision thresholds We assign each trace one of two labels, pass or fail. This is a binary pass/fail eval , which we recommend because it encourages clear criteria and is easier to align with human preferences. Each decision model returns a score from 0 to 1 that estimates how likely a trace is to contain a failure. The APIs turn this score into a decision using a default decision threshold of 0.50 . Traces with scores at or above the threshold are flagged as failures. Using this default without checking it against your data can give you subpar results. For example, a model could assign every failure a score of 0.40 and every passing trace a score of 0.10. Even though this model classifies traces perfectly at a threshold of 0.30, the default threshold of 0.50 would catch nothing. In practice, scores for failures and passing traces will overlap. Lowering the threshold catches more failures but can also raise more false alarms. Choosing a threshold means balancing: Precision: The share of flagged traces that contain a known failure. Recall: The share of known failures that the model catches. The right tradeoff depends on your business goals. For example, criminal trials set a high bar for conviction to avoid convicting innocent people, emphasizing precision. Cancer screening may emphasize recall, accepting more false alarms to miss fewer cases. 6 For this comparison, we’ll give precision and recall equal weight using the F1 score , their harmonic mean. F1 ranges from 0 to 1, and higher is better. The curves below show how each model scores failures (orange) and passing traces (blue). Taller parts of a curve mean more scores from that class fall in that range. Scores at or above the dashed threshold line are flagged. Use the toggle to compare 0.50 with Optimized for best F1 , which chooses a threshold for each model. 7 OpenAI separates the two classes best on this task, which is also reflected in its higher F1 score. It’s also important not to blindly maximize F1 without thinking about your minimum requirements for the classifier to be useful. For example, if this classifier is used for an automated alerting system, I would want a minimum of 80% on both precision and recall so that I’m minimizing false alarms while catching a sufficient number of failures. The chart below shows how precision and recall change at different thresholds. 8 The shaded region marks where both reach at least 80%. Perplexity, Liquid d1-ultra, and OpenAI Decisions meet our requirements, but we still need to choose a decision threshold within the shaded region for each model. In the next section, we’ll discuss how to tune those thresholds. Tuning the decision threshold For this example, we’ll optimize F1. For our candidates, we’ll restrict tuning to thresholds that meet both 80% minimums on the training data whenever possible. We leave the other models unconstrained to illustrate the effect of tuning. 9 With labeled traces and saved model scores, you can ask a coding agent to tune the thresholds. Below is an example prompt you can modify for your use case: Using my saved model scores and binary labels (1 means failure), tune a decision threshold to maximize F1 while requiring at least 80% precision and 80% recall. Use stratified five-fold cross-validation, choosing thresholds on the training examples and measuring performance on the remaining examples. If comparing models, use the same splits for each. Only select thresholds that meet both minimums on the training examples. If none qualifies, report that rather than relaxing either requirement. Report validation precision, recall, and F1, along with any splits where no threshold qualified or validation performance fell below my minimums. Compare with the default threshold of 0.50. Reuse the saved scores without making new model calls. Here’s how tuning for F1 changed each model’s performance. We group the three candidates from the precision-recall chart together and show the other models in gray to illustrate how much tuning can help. Our candidate models gained less from F1 tuning than Liquid d1 and Clef Flash, which fell below our minimums. However, even a small shift in precision and recall can affect business costs or the user experience, so choose the tradeoff deliberately. In practice, it’s unlikely that precision and recall are equally important (as we assumed in this post with F1). For example, the F-beta score lets you give precision more weight with beta below 1, or recall more weight with beta above 1. Optimizing a different metric could lead to different thresholds and results. Performance versus cost The chart below compares each model’s F1 (after tuning) against cost, focused on our remaining candidates: The dashed line shows the Pareto frontier among our remaining candidates. For any given F1 score, it identifies the cheapest candidate that meets or exceeds that score. This particular chart is a bit silly as there are only three options, but it’s a useful illustration for how to think about cost vs. performance. Perplexity was the cheapest of these candidates at 0.82 cents per 100 eval runs, with an F1 of 0.79. OpenAI Decisions reached an F1 of 0.87 at 3.72 cents per 100 eval runs, about 4.5 times the cost. Can we trust the probabilities? Beyond pass/fail evals, you may want to use a decision model’s score as a confidence estimate. But can you take that number literally? For a score of 0.80 to mean an 80% chance of failure, roughly 80% of traces with similar scores should contain failures. The chart below shows each model’s probability calibration : how closely its predicted probabilities match observed outcomes. 10 Each point represents about 20 traces with similar scores. A point on the diagonal means the predicted probability matches the failure rate in that group. Above the line, the model underestimates the risk of failure. Below it, the model overestimates that risk. If the predicted probabilities don’t match the observed outcomes, we can adjust them using another model. The second panel shows one method, Platt scaling , which fits a simple curve to make that adjustment. 11 Perplexity, Liquid d1, and Clef Flash move closer to the diagonal after calibration. For example, one group of Clef Flash traces had an average predicted failure probability of about 8%, but 60% contained failures. Jev and Liquid d1-ultra were already well calibrated on this dataset and needed little adjustment. Platt scaling isn’t always the best fit. For example, OpenAI’s probabilities got slightly worse with the version of Platt scaling we used. 12 You can direct your coding agent to perform calibration with the following prompt: Using my saved failure probabilities and binary labels (1 means failure), test whether Platt scaling improves each model’s probabilities. Use stratified five-fold cross-validation with the same splits for every model. Fit the calibration mapping on each training split and apply it to the remaining traces. Fit on log-odds, clipping probabilities away from 0 and 1 first. Plot predicted probabilities against observed failure rates before and after calibration. Report Brier scores (lower is better), and explain which models improved or got worse. Reuse the saved scores without making new model calls. Prompt tuning and evaluator scope We kept the eval task in this post broad to make the differences between models easier to see. In practice, we recommend building a separate judge for each failure mode . With a narrower task and more specific guidance, we expect the performance gaps between models to shrink. I like to start with a larger model that has acceptable performance on a task and then try smaller models to see if they can match the larger model’s performance for less cost. Prompt tuning can also be helpful if you have high-quality labels. 13 I discuss how to craft a good judge prompt in this post . Putting these ideas into practice For this particular dataset, OpenAI had breakout performance at a higher cost. Perplexity and Liquid d1-ultra offer lower-cost options with lower performance. We have observed that model performance varies substantially across tasks and datasets, which means it’s important to measure things yourself. To recap: Once you’re satisfied with your judge’s prompt , set minimum precision and recall requirements for your use case. Rule out models that cannot meet these. Tune each model’s decision threshold before comparing performance. Choose a precision-recall tradeoff that fits your business goals. Be intentional, don’t just use F1 score because this post did! If you want to use scores as confidence estimates, check whether the probabilities match observed outcomes. Calibration can help, but you need to measure whether it improves them. Weigh performance against cost and latency for your workload. This process is iterative. You may improve the prompt, then need to tune the threshold again or revisit calibration. In this post, we focused on threshold tuning and calibration because we’ve seen many people use decision models off the shelf without considering these factors. You might also be wondering how decision models stack up to LLMs. OpenAI Decisions uses GPT-6 Luna, which delivered our highest F1 at the highest cost, suggesting that harder eval tasks may justify paying more for an LLM. In a broader comparison , Randy Olson found that decision models could match LLMs on classification and routing at lower cost, while LLMs pulled ahead on tasks requiring knowledge and reasoning. None of the ideas discussed in this post are new. Choosing a precision-recall tradeoff, tuning thresholds and comparing performance vs. cost are part of evaluating any classifier. To learn more about these fundamentals, I recommend Machine Learning with Python Cookbook, 2nd Edition by Kyle Gallatin and Chris Albon. Finally, if you’re a data scientist or ML engineer wondering where you belong in the AI age, these are skills you already have. It’s time to get revenge 🙂. Appendix: Evaluation prompt Perplexity, Liquid d1 and d1-ultra, Clef Flash, and OpenAI Decisions received the prompt below. Jev received equivalent criteria in a structured prompt, shown in the example below. The scores and labels used in the charts are available as JSON. Decide whether `messages` contains at least one substantive failure, risk, or quality problem in the AI assistant's behavior or tool use. This is one complete production trace from an AI that handles apartment-leasing customer support over phone or messaging. The trace includes the conversation plus any tool calls and tool outputs. Evaluate the AI assistant and its tool use, not the customer. Treat system messages inside `messages` as the instructions governing the assistant's behavior and allowed capabilities. Inspect the full trace, including final turns and all tool calls and outputs. Base the judgment only on evidence visible in this trace. Do not assume external policies, channel behavior, or business requirements that are not present. Do not assume every trace failed. A short, ambiguous, or inconclusive trace is not an issue unless visible evidence establishes a substantive failure. Return the probability that at least one substantive issue is present; the issue does not need to be named or clustered. Count as an issue when supported by the trace: the assistant contradicts an applicable system instruction or tool result; makes an unsupported factual or operational claim; misses, misuses, repeats, or falsely claims completion of a required tool action, transfer, booking, cancellation, follow-up, or confirmation; materially misunderstands or leaves an explicit user request unresolved; or exposes internal actions, placeholders, or broken content to the customer in a way that materially harms the interaction. Do not count as an issue: a minor stylistic preference with no meaningful effect; a failure caused only by the customer's behavior; internal tool metadata that was not exposed to the customer and did not cause an incorrect response; a hypothetical concern requiring information outside the trace; or insufficient evidence and inconclusive conversations. Note Example: A structured prompt This is how we structured the prompt for Jev’s requests, with separate fields for instructions and evaluation criteria. { "version" : "nurtureboss-any-issue-v1" , "question_id" : "has_substantive_issue" , "type" : "noul" , "instructions" : { "task" : "Does `messages` contain at least one substantive failure, risk, or quality problem in the AI assistant's behavior or tool use?" , "context" : "This is one production trace from an AI that handles apartment-leasing customer support over phone or messaging. The trace contains the complete conversation plus any tool calls and tool outputs." , "evaluation_rules" : [ "Evaluate the AI assistant and its tool use, not the customer." , "Treat system messages inside `messages` as the instructions governing the assistant's behavior and allowed capabilities." , "Inspect the full trace, including the final turns and all tool calls and outputs." , "Base the judgment only on evidence visible in this trace. Do not assume external policies, channel behavior, or business requirements that are not present." , "Do not assume every trace failed. A short, ambiguous, or inconclusive trace is not an issue unless the visible evidence establishes a substantive failure." , "Return the probability that at least one substantive issue is present. The issue does not need to be named or clustered." ] }, "criteria" : { "true" : { "definition" : "At least one substantive problem is supported by evidence in the trace." , "examples_of_qualifying_evidence" : [ "The assistant contradicts an applicable system instruction or a tool result." , "The assistant makes an unsupported factual or operational claim." , "A required tool action, transfer, booking, cancellation, follow-up, or confirmation is missing, incorrect, repeated, or falsely claimed as complete." , "The assistant materially misunderstands or leaves an explicit user request unresolved." , "Customer-facing text exposes internal actions, placeholders, or broken content that materially harms the interaction." ] }, "false" : { "definition" : "No substantive assistant problem can be established from the visible trace." , "do_not_count_as_an_issue" : [ "A minor stylistic preference with no meaningful effect." , "A failure caused only by the customer's behavior." , "Internal tool metadata that was not exposed to the customer and did not cause an incorrect response." , "A hypothetical concern that requires information outside the trace." , "Insufficient evidence or an inconclusive conversation." ] } } } Footnotes Versions tested: Jev 1.13 ( announced September 15, 2026 ), Perplexity Decider 1.1 27B , Liquid d1 and d1-ultra , Cloudflare Clef Flash , and OpenAI Decisions . OpenAI Decisions uses GPT-6 Luna. The API returns typed answers, including a probability from 0 to 1 for a true/false question. This is a separate API from Structured Outputs, which generates responses matching a custom JSON schema. We include it because it serves the same classification task.↩︎ An LLM judge uses a prompt to evaluate an AI system’s output or behavior. We recommend asking it for a binary pass/fail decision about a specific failure mode. This encourages clear criteria and makes it easier to compare the judge’s decisions with human labels.↩︎ We scored 98 production traces after excluding two internal QA examples from the 100-trace dataset. The frozen reference contains 61 known failures and 37 traces without a labeled failure: 39 failures from the original human review plus 22 discoveries from Braintrust and Arize that we manually validated. Models received masked traces without human labels or reviewer notes. Perplexity, Liquid, Clef Flash, and OpenAI received the same instructions and serialized inputs; Jev received equivalent criteria through its structured API. The original conversations are private.↩︎ API cost covers 100 eval runs, one per trace. We use Liquid’s prices as of October 17, 2026 , $0.02 per million input tokens for d1 and $0.042 for d1-ultra. The experiment recorded d1 at $0.04; we have repriced its saved token usage. Other models use the rates in the experiment’s operational metrics. Performance excludes two internal QA traces. Threshold tuning uses saved scores and requires no additional model calls.↩︎ Latency depends on how you batch or parallelize requests, your arrangement with the vendor, and your distance from its infrastructure, among other factors. Batching and concurrency can also change cost and throughput. See TypeSafe’s multi-question requests and client performance guidance . Its launch discussion also notes the location of its latency tests relative to its service. Mean response times were 4.33 seconds for Jev, 7.85 for Perplexity, 7.38 for Liquid d1, 1.56 for Liquid d1-ultra, 2.09 for Clef Flash, and 2.77 for OpenAI. These came from separate runs and do not establish comparative throughput or tail latency.↩︎ These examples illustrate how the consequences of mistakes affect the tradeoff. In U.S. criminal trials, proof beyond a reasonable doubt sets a high bar for conviction. In cancer screening, a missed case can delay care, while a false alarm can lead to anxiety and unnecessary procedures. A positive screening result usually requires further testing. The NCI explains both risks ; the appropriate balance depends on the screening test and population.↩︎ The density plots show unconstrained F1 tuning, before we introduce minimum precision and recall requirements. The later comparison charts apply those requirements to candidate models where feasible. All use the same five-fold cross-validation splits. Thresholds were chosen on training traces, and precision, recall, and F1 were measured on separate traces. We average those measurements across repeated splits. In the optimized density plots, the dashed line shows the average selected threshold. The displayed scores come from the individual splits, rather than applying that average threshold to the full dataset. The density curves use Gaussian smoothing with bandwidth 0.07 and reflection at 0 and 1. Each class has an area of one. Smoothing affects only the display.↩︎ A precision-recall curve plots precision against recall as the decision threshold changes. It shows the tradeoffs available for a model across thresholds. Scikit-learn’s precision-recall guide explains how to read and plot these curves.↩︎ We identify candidates from the full-sample precision-recall curves. In each training split, we choose the highest-F1 threshold among those reaching at least 80% precision and 80% recall. When no threshold qualifies, we use the unconstrained F1 optimum and record the split as infeasible. This occurred in 36 of 100 training splits for Perplexity and 29 for Liquid d1-ultra, and never for OpenAI. Non-candidates always use unconstrained F1 tuning. We keep all validation predictions, including those from fallback splits, in the reported averages. The minimums apply during selection and do not guarantee the same performance on new examples. The threshold-selection audit records each split without trace IDs.↩︎ A calibrated failure probability of 0.80 means that, among many examples receiving scores near 0.80, roughly 80% contain failures. Platt scaling and isotonic regression use labeled examples to learn an adjustment from model scores to probabilities. Platt scaling fits a sigmoid curve. Isotonic regression fits a more flexible mapping that preserves score order, but is more prone to overfitting with small datasets. Neither guarantees improvement on new examples. Scikit-learn’s probability calibration guide explains both methods and how to assess them.↩︎ The reliability chart groups each model’s scores into five groups of 19 or 20 traces, sorted by probability. The adjusted scores are each trace’s mean out-of-fold probability from the saved cross-validation results. We fit Platt scaling to the log-odds of the original probabilities. Each mapping is fitted without the traces it predicts. The chart summarizes this small sample and does not establish an exact failure rate for a future trace. The plotted calibration results are available as JSON.↩︎ On the saved out-of-fold probability summaries, Jev’s Brier score was 0.187 before adjustment and 0.188 afterward. Liquid d1-ultra’s was 0.173 and 0.172, while OpenAI’s was 0.159 and 0.164. Brier score measures average squared probability error, so lower is better. It reflects discrimination as well as calibration. These results describe the log-odds Platt fit shown in the chart. An exploratory refit directly on probabilities, using the same folds, gave OpenAI a Brier score of 0.154. This illustrates sensitivity to the fitting method. It does not establish which method will work best on new data.↩︎ GEPA uses feedback from model runs to propose prompt revisions and test them against labeled examples. It retains candidates with different strengths, so a prompt that helps a difficult example can remain in consideration. Incorrect labels can steer this search toward the wrong changes. Keep a separate test set outside prompt development for the final check. In our small manual Jev experiment, F1 at the default threshold rose from 0.78 with a simple prompt to 0.80 with a checklist of failure types. That experiment did not use GEPA or establish how much systematic optimization would help. Our FAQ on choosing an eval model discusses prompt optimization and model comparison.↩︎

items.title: AI for Science expands to foundations and research institutions
items.full_text:
We’re highlighting 20 scientific foundations, institutions, and research groups from around the world that we’ve partnered with in an expansion of our AI for Science program, which gives free Claude credits to researchers working on high-impact scientific projects.
We started the AI for Science program in May 2025 with the belief that AI could significantly speed up scientific progress. Our goal is to increase access to AI tools and resources to enable researchers to deepen and expand their own scientific work. (Over the last few months, we’ve also launched our discounted Team plan for scientists and have supported hundreds of projects across biology, medicine, physics, chemistry, climate science, and mathematics.)
Scientists have told us that they’re working with Claude to generate hypotheses, design experiments, swiftly analyze complex data, and communicate findings. With scientists at the center of this transformation, the field is setting the questions and developing the research projects that will help us tackle some of humanity’s toughest problems.
Over the past year, we’ve started to expand this work and partner with scientific organizations to build collaborative research projects. For instance, we partnered with HHMI Janelia Research Campus to develop the Model Hardware Standard (MHS), a shared specification that lets AI agents safely operate lab instruments. MHS is currently in research preview. We also support the Allen Institute, a leader in creating large open datasets and tools to advance research on the brain, cells, and the immune system. The institute is building teams of AI agents to analyze that data, turning months of manual analysis into hours.
AI for Science began by supporting individual scientists. By partnering with institutions and foundations, we’re now able to reach more researchers across many fields. Many of these projects will also produce public goods that benefit the wider scientific community: open datasets, open-source software, open standards, and shared libraries. We look forward to seeing how AI resources can expand what scientists can attempt and lead to new discoveries.

The discount also extends to state, local, tribal and territorial governments.
We are also launching a dedicated program to help agencies implement and make the most of their Claude use. These programs are commonly leveraged by our private sector customers and we’re looking forward to bringing those best practices to our public sector partners in the coming weeks.
Approximately 500 US federal, state, and local government organizations now use Claude. Weekly Claude for Government active users are up about eightfold since February, and usage across federal civilian agencies has grown about 20-fold in a year. Those organizations run some of the most important systems in the country, usually on tight budgets and with long procurement cycles. This agreement is built to support that work, so they can apply Claude to hard problems without a large upfront commitment.

items.title: Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation
items.full_text:
Today, we’re donating Agent Skills, the open standard that gives AI agents specialized knowledge and workflows, to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF). More than 70 agent platforms, including ChatGPT, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, and VS Code, have integrated Agent Skills since we published the standard in December 2025.
Agent interoperability through simplicity
A skill is a folder containing a SKILL.md file that teaches an agent a specific task or domain, along with any scripts or reference material it needs. We developed skills while working on Claude Code. It handled general knowledge work well, but often lacked the procedural knowledge that real business tasks need. Within weeks of our October 2025 launch, developers published thousands of skills on GitHub and wrote loaders for Codex, Cursor, and OpenCode. We then published Agent Skills as an open standard, under its own GitHub organization and domain, so any agent could use it. So far, 1 million skills have been published and nearly 280 million installed.
Donating Agent Skills to AAIF
We’re committed to keeping Agent Skills open, community-driven, and vendor-neutral. Today, we are donating the standard to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) under the Linux Foundation, which we co-founded with Block and OpenAI last year, and to which we donated the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The AAIF will provide a neutral home to the standard going forward, ensuring the community has a say in where Agent Skills go next.
We are donating the Agent Skills name and logo, the GitHub organization, and the agentskills.io domain. You can continue to use the standard or contribute to it without joining the AAIF.
Engineers from Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, and other companies will maintain the standard as individuals, with David Soria Parra and Mahesh Murag as Lead Maintainers.
What comes next
We’ve proposed starting with a roadmap covering versioned releases, a formal proposal process, and security guidance for people who write and install skills. As with MCP, the project will continue to prioritize community input and transparent decision-making. You can join the project’s Discord to give feedback on proposed specification changes.
Thank you to the developers who built with Agent Skills from the start, and to the teams who brought skills into their products. Read the specification at agentskills.io and join the discussion on GitHub.

items.title: Open call for guest investigators in the life sciences
items.full_text:
Today, we’re inviting members of the life sciences community to apply to work with us on special projects. We’re looking for proposals from principal investigators and their research groups at academic institutions, nonprofits, or government labs who want to use Claude to investigate key questions in causal human biology, structural and computational molecular biology, medicinal chemistry, drug discovery, and clinical science.
You can submit a proposal for a project here.
Over 8–12 weeks, guest investigators will work directly with Anthropic researchers on a problem of interest and produce the analyses, artifacts, and tools that will be most helpful for them in their work. Our team will run our models and harnesses at no cost to them.
We’ll work together to publish these outputs and open-source the accompanying data and code. Guest investigators retain the rights to their data at every step during their project. They will also have the rights to any independent follow-on research that might come out of our collaboration.
We’re looking for applicants who can clearly explain how they would benefit from direct collaboration with Anthropic’s researchers. Applicants should also make a reasonable case that their outputs (e.g., preliminary discoveries, answers to open questions, open-source datasets, or public resources) can be produced within the 8- to 12-week collaboration period. There may be an option for extension beyond the initial collaboration period for some projects.
We understand that the results for most open problems of interest will take much longer to validate, but we’re looking for proposals that can produce some preliminary evidence in a relatively short amount of time.
We aren’t asking for guest investigators to give us their data, either in the application or during the collaboration, and we’re requesting that applicants include only publicly available information in their application materials.
Applications will be open for approximately 14 days, and we’ll strive to notify selected participants by email approximately 14 days after applications close. We look forward to potentially expanding this effort in the future as we learn more about how we can best support the scientific community.
This program is one of several initiatives Anthropic is pursuing to invest more heavily in the life sciences and the broader scientific research community. Scientists who would like direct access to our most capable publicly available models for biology can apply to join our Life Sciences Verification Program. We’ve also continued to support researchers through our AI for Science initiative, which provides scientists with Claude credits to accelerate their progress toward making scientific discoveries.

items.title: Physicist Christopher Stubbs joins Anthropic's Long-Term Benefit Trust
items.full_text:
Dr. Christopher Stubbs, an experimental physicist and former Dean of Science at Harvard University, has joined Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust. He brings to the Trust decades of scientific expertise across observational cosmology and precision measurement. He has also advised the US government on national security and arms control.
“I am honored to join Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust and to help the company deliver on its public benefit mission,” said Stubbs. “I use AI tools in my research every day and see what they make possible, and as an educator I have confronted some of the hard questions they raise. As a grandfather, I want to help ensure that AI is developed and deployed for the long-term benefit of humanity.”
Stubbs is the Samuel C. Moncher Professor of Physics and of Astronomy at Harvard, where he served as Dean of Science from 2018 to 2024. In 1998, as a member of the High-Z Supernova Search Team, he helped discover the accelerating expansion of the universe, work that later earned the team the Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics. He was also the inaugural project scientist for what is now the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which started a 10-year survey of the southern sky in June. One of its aims is to study the accelerating expansion he helped discover.
More recently, he’s written about how to keep AI-assisted research reproducible when models can give different answers to the same question. He’s a member of JASON, an independent group of scientists who have advised the US government on defense and technology since 1960.
“When Chris found evidence that the universe was expanding at a rate no one expected, he and his team followed the data even when it went against the prevailing wisdom of the field. As AI starts to transform how science itself is done, Chris’s intellectual honesty, rigor, and commitment to the truth are the values we want shaping the future of this technology, and I’m grateful he’s bringing his deep expertise to the Trust,” said Daniela Amodei, Co-founder and President of Anthropic.
Anthropic is a Public Benefit Corporation, which means we’re structured to balance commercial growth with our public benefit purpose. The Trust exists to help us hold that balance over the long term. It has the authority to appoint a majority of Anthropic’s board, and Trustees advise the board and our leadership on critical decisions, particularly those involving risks and societal impacts of AI.
This week we published our first Public Benefit Report, a public account of how we’re working toward our charter and where we’re falling short. The Trustees helped define the five charter pillars it measures us against, and the report closes with their assessment of our progress to date. Subject to stockholder approval, we’ve also committed to setting aside a portion of Anthropic’s shares to Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a new entity with a structure that increases the stake as the company grows.
